Male Black goby (Gobius niger) reach a maximum total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the Gobiidae in Mediterranean coastal ecosystems. This ultimate length is achieved only after several years of growth, and individuals attaining this size are typically dominant males occupying prime nesting sites in shallow, structured habitats such as seagrass beds or rocky crevices. The length-weight relationship for this species indicates that a male of this maximal length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 63.3 grams [Wwi = 63.3 grams], a body mass that reflects the considerable energetic investment in somatic growth and territorial defense. Females, by contrast, generally remain somewhat smaller, though sexual size dimorphism is not extreme. These upper size limits are frequently documented in field surveys of populations inhabiting the Adriatic and Aegean Seas, where stable environmental conditions permit extended growth trajectories. The asymptotic body size appears to be constrained by both metabolic demands and the availability of suitable spawning substrates, as competition for high-quality nesting cavities intensifies among larger individuals. Age determination from otolith readings confirms that only a fraction of the male population ever reaches this terminal size, with many succumbing to predation or senescence before attaining full growth potential.

At the opposite end of the life cycle, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva of Gobius niger emerges from the egg at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00016 grams [Wwb = just 0.00016 grams]. This minute initial mass is a direct consequence of the egg dimensions, which measure approximately 1.5 millimeters in length and 0.45 millimeters in width, resulting in an ellipsoidal volume that yields this low starting weight. Upon eclosion, the prolarva is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, and the period of lecithotrophic existence lasts for several days until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The yolk-sac stage is a critical bottleneck in the early life history, as the tiny larva must rapidly develop the capacity to capture planktonic prey before its finite energy stores are exhausted. Mortality during this interval is exceptionally high, a common pattern among marine teleosts with pelagic larvae, and only a minute fraction of hatchlings survive to the juvenile phase. The reduced birth mass, relative to demersal egg layers in other families, underscores an r-selected reproductive strategy in which high fecundity compensates for extreme early-life attrition, a trade-off that is fundamental to the species' population dynamics in variable coastal environments.

Sexual maturation in Gobius niger is attained at a relatively modest size compared to the ultimate length. Puberty is reached when individuals achieve a total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 2.4 grams [Wwp = 2.4 grams] based on the established length-weight relationship. At this developmental milestone, the gonads become active, and both sexes begin to exhibit courtship behaviors associated with the upcoming spawning season. In males, the onset of reproductive maturity is also marked by a pronounced darkening of body coloration and the development of a distinctive white margin on the dorsal fin, signals that are used in territorial displays and mate attraction. The time required to reach this pubertal stage is approximately 292 days since birth [tp = approximately 292 days since birth] under stable thermal conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a duration that allows a single cohort to recruit into the adult population within their first year of life. This relatively rapid maturation facilitates a high turnover rate in populations subject to seasonal fluctuations in food availability and predation pressure. The energetic investment required to achieve puberty, from the initial 0.00016 gram larva to a 2.4 gram reproductive adult, represents an enormous multiplier in body mass and a testament to the efficiency of the species' growth physiology.

The reproductive biology of Gobius niger is characterized by a high potential output, with females capable of producing up to 16 eggs per day [Ri = up to 16 eggs per day] under optimal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This daily fecundity represents a maximum daily reproduction rate that allows females to deposit successive clutches of adhesive, demersal eggs inside sheltered nests, typically beneath stones or within empty bivalve shells, where males then guard the developing embryos until hatching. Females produce multiple clutches per spawning season, distributing their reproductive effort across several cycles, a strategy that mitigates the risk of total brood loss to stochastic environmental events. Field observations indicate that larger, older females contribute disproportionately to total egg production, as their greater body size permits larger clutch volumes and higher daily egg deposition rates, reinforcing the importance of protecting mature individuals for population sustainability.

Longevity data for Gobius niger indicate a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] when held under controlled laboratory conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], though wild individuals likely experience somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation and environmental stressors. This five-year life expectancy is typical of small-bodied benthic gobies and reflects a life history strategy that balances relatively early maturation, high fecundity, and a moderately extended reproductive window. Males that survive to older ages often occupy the most favorable nesting territories and may exhibit greater reproductive success through both mate guarding and nest defense. Senescence in older individuals manifests as reduced swimming performance, slower predator evasion, and lower feeding efficiency, ultimately leading to increased natural mortality. The stable thermal conditions used in laboratory studies approximate the annual mean water temperature in many of the species' shallow coastal habitats, where seasonal variation is moderate but extended cold spells or heatwaves can influence metabolic rates and growth trajectories. Comparative studies with other Gobiidae, such as Gobius paganellus, reveal that the lifespan of Gobius niger is intermediate, aligning with its position along a latitudinal gradient where slower-growing, northern populations may exhibit somewhat greater longevity. The interplay between temperature regime, food supply, and reproductive investment ultimately dictates the realized lifespan in any given population, highlighting the phenotypic plasticity inherent in this adaptable benthic fish.
